t: Process Restricted Friend Requests: Union-Find with Restriction Checks
o:
**Understanding the problem**

We manage `n` people who initially have no friendships, a list of restricted pairs that must never end up in the same friend group (directly or indirectly), and an ordered list of friend requests. Processing request `(u, v)` asks whether merging the friend circles of `u` and `v` would put any restricted pair into one circle: if so the request fails, otherwise it succeeds and the merge becomes permanent. In Example 3, request `[0, 4]` succeeds and merges `{0, 4}`; `[1, 2]` fails because it is itself restricted; `[3, 1]` succeeds because no restriction spans those two circles, giving `{1, 3}`; finally `[3, 4]` fails because restriction `(0, 1)` would become connected via `4 - 3 - 1 - 0`. Since `n`, the number of requests, and the number of restrictions are all at most 1000, re-examining every restriction for every request (about 10^6 checks) is comfortably fast.
k: Friendship is transitive: accepting a request merges two entire components, so component membership matters, not direct edges.
Request `(u, v)` is safe iff no restriction `(x, y)` straddles the two components: `x` grouped with `u` while `y` is grouped with `v`, or vice versa.
Union-Find makes each connectivity test and merge nearly constant time, reducing every request to one scan over the restrictions.

a.n: Approach 1: Recompute Components with BFS per Request
a.i: Without any specialized structure, rebuild the whole component labeling by BFS over the accumulated friendship adjacency list for every request. The request fails exactly when some restriction has one endpoint in u's fresh component and the other in v's.
s: Keep an adjacency list of accepted friendships.
For each request, run BFS from every unvisited person to label all components.
Reject iff some restriction (x, y) has comp[x] == comp[u] and comp[y] == comp[v], or the symmetric case.
Otherwise accept, add edge u-v, and record true.
a.t: O(q * (n + q + r)) — each of the q requests triggers a full BFS over up to n nodes and accumulated edges, plus a scan of r restrictions
a.sp: O(n + q) — adjacency list plus component-label array

a.i: Maintain components incrementally with DSU instead of rebuilding them. Invariant: accepted components never contain a restricted pair internally, so a merge of roots ru and rv is unsafe only when some restriction already has one endpoint rooted at ru and the other at rv. One linear scan of the restrictions per request settles it.
s: For each request compute ru = find(u) and rv = find(v).
Scan restrictions: reject if find(x) == ru && find(y) == rv, or find(x) == rv && find(y) == ru, for some (x, y).
If safe, union ru and rv and answer true.
a.t: O(r * q * a(n)) — every request scans all r restrictions; each find/union runs in amortized near-constant inverse-Ackermann time

w:
**Wrap-up**

Present the DSU solution in an interview; the BFS baseline mainly motivates the key invariant that accepted components stay restriction-free. Pitfalls: rejecting a repeated request between current friends (their roots are equal, so no restriction can span them and the answer must be true); checking whether x and y relate to each other instead of specifically to u and v; and merging before the restriction scan finishes. Follow-ups: handling friendship deletions (needs offline processing or weighted DSU variants), or reporting which restriction caused each rejection.
